transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-05-06 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Alex Reed (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Stonegate VP Eng), Maya Ortiz (Stonegate Head Platform), Ethan Cole (Stonegate Dir Security), Liam Park (Cloud Infra)

Summary: quick intro, scope network options for Private/VPC deployment (peering vs private endpoints vs Transit Gateway), region constraints (Azure vs AWS), egress IP, KMS/encryption, audit logs, timeline and next steps.

00:00:08 Alex Reed: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on this account. We're joined by Priya and Samir on the technical side. Jordan, Maya, Ethan - great to meet you. Can you do quick intros?
00:00:20 Jordan Lee: Yeah, Jordan, VP Eng at Stonegate. We run internal ops for both our customer-facing apps and grid analytics. Maya's the platform lead, Ethan runs security. Liam's our infra guy.
00:00:34 Maya Ortiz: Hi all. We're evaluating Redwood for inference serving of our forecasting models - main ask is private VPC deployment due to data residency and contractual controls.
00:00:44 Priya Nair: Great, thanks. We'll focus this call on networking and compliance constraints, and we can map out what Private looks like vs Dedicated/Hosted.
00:01:02 Samir Patel: Quick note - we often recommend starting with a small pilot in Private and then expand. But let's hear your constraints first.

00:01:28 Jordan Lee: High level constraints: data can't cross our AWS accounts; all egress must go through our corporate egress appliances; most workloads are in us-east-1 and eu-west-1; need KMS control for model input encryption and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. Timeline 3-6 months if pilot goes well.
00:01:50 Ethan Cole: Also SOC2 requirements and SAML SSO for ops access. We need the ability to rotate keys and see who accessed model endpoints.
00:02:05 Alex Reed: Makes sense. For Private we offer a few patterns: 1) VPC peering from your VPC to the Redwood VPC in your account (cross-account peering), 2) Private endpoints / interface endpoints into Redwood services, or 3) Transit Gateway hub for multi-region routing - each has tradeoffs.
00:02:28 Maya Ortiz: Can you run through the tradeoffs? Especially around cross-account peering and egress control - we can't have unexpected internet routes.
00:02:40 Priya Nair: Sure. With straight VPC peering it's simpler and lower latency - it's direct L3 peering - but it's per-region and you manage the route tables. For many customers we do cross-account peering where Redwood deploys a VPC in their account or we peer into Redwood-managed account depending on the model.
00:03:04 Samir Patel: The other option is creating AWS PrivateLink-style interface endpoints. That avoids some of the routing complexity and gives you endpoint ENIs in your subnet. Downside is slightly higher latency and you need to manage endpoint policies and quotas.
00:03:23 Jordan Lee: What about Transit Gateway? We have a TGW already and a lot of spoke VPCs. Would that work?
00:03:30 Priya Nair: Yes, TGW is often preferred for larger orgs - you can centralize routing and enforce egress through your appliances. Redwood can peer our VPCs into your TGW or deploy stack in your account attached to TGW. There's a bit more setup on both sides but it's more scalable.
00:03:52 Ethan Cole: Important: all egress must go through our Palo Alto appliances, and we need static egress IPs so our partners can whitelist them. Can Redwood provide stable egress ranges?
00:04:07 Alex Reed: For Private deployments running in your VPC (customer-owned) egress is controlled by you - so stable IPs are your responsibility. If using Redwood-hosted Private where we manage the VPC, we can provide published egress IP ranges per region, but for strict whitelisting we recommend the customer-owned VPC pattern.
00:04:29 Maya Ortiz: Ok that aligns with our preference to keep networking inside our account. Are there options to bring our own KMS/HSM?
00:04:38 Priya Nair: Yes. We integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping. You can manage CMKs in your account and Redwood will be configured to use them for at-rest model artifacts and optionally request-level encryption. There are some operational caveats around key rotation windows that we'll document.
00:04:55 Liam Park: When you say Redwood 'uses' our KMS - does any plaintext ever leave our account? We need to avoid that.
00:05:02 Samir Patel: Good question. For the customer-owned deployment pattern, model artifacts and I/O can stay encrypted in your S3 and only decrypted by the compute nodes in the same account. We can also support envelope encryption so direct plaintext is minimized. I'll follow up with our security pack with detail.

00:05:30 Jordan Lee: Region constraints - our regulatory team requires EU data to stay in eu-west-1 for certain customers. Can we pin deployments to regions?
00:05:40 Priya Nair: Absolutely - you can pin model endpoints to a particular region. For high availability we can do multi-region standby but for strict residency we keep endpoints and storage in the same region. Be mindful of cold-start latency if you do separate region models.
00:05:58 Maya Ortiz: Any limits on instance types / GPUs if we deploy in our VPC?
00:06:05 Samir Patel: You can select instance families we support - our runtime supports A100, H100, and some RTX profiles depending on the AMI and region. If a region doesn't have the desired GPU historically we can suggest compatible flavors or consider Dedicated pockets in a region that does. We'll include a matrix.

00:06:30 Ethan Cole: About logs/audit: we need per-request audit logs, user identity tracing (SAML subject), and retention at our SIEM. Can Redwood push logs directly to a Kinesis or an S3 bucket in our account?
00:06:44 Priya Nair: Yes, log forwarding into your account is supported: CloudWatch logs, Kinesis Firehose, or direct S3 export. We can also add structured request metadata for tracing and include SAML subject if you're using SSO. We'll need an IAM role to assume for that.
00:07:02 Jordan Lee: Does Redwood support private DNS resolution so internal hostnames resolve to the interface endpoints?
00:07:10 Samir Patel: We can publish private DNS entries via Route53 private hosted zones when using PrivateLink or when we've deployed within your account we'll recommend using your internal DNS. There are some gotchas with split-horizon DNS which we'll document.

00:07:38 Maya Ortiz: On cost - there's the hosted per-token model, then Dedicated reserved capacity, and then Private (customer VPC) which I assume is a licensing/infra + support arrangement. What's the unit economics?
00:07:50 Alex Reed: Private typically has a platform fee plus the infra costs you incur. Dedicated is a reserved Redwood capacity with commit pricing. Hosted is pure usage. For large, steady workloads Private or Dedicated usually lowers overall unit cost because you control the infra and get better GPU packing. We'll follow up with ballpark numbers based on your expected QPS.
00:08:10 Jordan Lee: We might start with a small Dedicated pool to evaluate latency and cost, then migrate to Private in our account if security gating is strict. Is that a path you support?
00:08:19 Priya Nair: Yes, customers do a staged approach: hosted for quick POC, Dedicated for production-ish tests, then Private for regulated workloads. We'll outline the migration path and what model version pinning looks like.

00:08:42 Maya Ortiz: Networking detail question: our VPCs use overlapping CIDRs with some partners - can Redwood handle NAT and route isolation appropriately?
00:08:52 Samir Patel: Overlapping CIDRs are a common friction. For peering, overlapping blocks won't route; we'd use NATs or deploy customer-owned placement in your account so the overlap doesn't matter. Another pattern is using Transit VPC and NAT gateway translations. We'll propose options once we see your CIDRs.

00:09:12 Ethan Cole: Any compliance packages for regulated industries? I'm particularly looking for evidence around change control, access reviews, and incident response integration.
00:09:22 Alex Reed: We have a compliance pack including SOC2 report, ISO summaries, pen test summary, and our incident response playbook. For Private deployments we can provide additional SLAs and runbooks. I'll include the pack in the follow-up email.

00:09:40 Jordan Lee: What about model weights / customer data retention - can Redwood guarantee deletion with proof? We have contracts requiring proof of deletion.
00:09:49 Priya Nair: We support retention policies and can provide certificate-style deletion proofs for stored artifacts. If everything runs in your account you control S3 lifecycle, but we can also produce logs of deletion actions when Redwood-managed.

00:10:10 Liam Park: For the pilot we'd like to run our forecasting model against a redwood endpoint with a synthetic dataset and measure p99 latency and token cost. How do we set that up?
00:10:20 Samir Patel: We can spin a small test cluster in your account or use a Dedicated test pool. We'll create a benchmark plan: sample payloads, QPS targets, and metrics we capture. Priya will own the plan.
00:10:33 Priya Nair: I'll send a benchmark template and we can schedule a 90-minute tech deep dive to run through infra details. 90-minute session ideally with your infra and security folks.

00:10:50 Alex Reed: Anything around SSO/SAML provisioning? How do you want operator access managed?
00:10:56 Ethan Cole: We require SSO for any ops level access. RBAC minimum privileged roles, and SCIM provisioning for user lifecycle would be ideal.
00:11:05 Priya Nair: Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. When deployed in private we can configure auth to federate to your IdP and map groups to RBAC roles. We'll include a diagram of the auth flow.

00:11:28 Jordan Lee: A couple of gotchas: we have some on-prem air-gapped sites - do you support any on-prem package?
00:11:35 Samir Patel: We do have an on-prem option (air-gapped) but it's heavier - package installation, ops runbooks, and our private control plane integration vary. For now, if you can run in cloud accounts that's simpler. For truly air-gapped we can discuss a separate engagement.

00:11:58 Maya Ortiz: Ok good. Can you summarize expected deliverables after this meeting?
00:12:04 Alex Reed: Sure - we'll send: 1) Security & compliance pack, 2) Network pattern doc with peering/TGW/PrivateLink options, 3) Pricing estimates for Dedicated vs Private, 4) Benchmark plan and template, 5) Proposed dates for tech deep dive.
00:12:20 Jordan Lee: Great. Any blockers from Redwood side?
00:12:23 Priya Nair: Nothing blockers we can't handle. We'll need your CIDR ranges, AWS account IDs, and compliance checklist to finalize patterns.

00:12:35 Ethan Cole: We'll share a short compliance checklist - data residency, KMS policies, retention, required logging, and key rotation windows.

00:12:45 Alex Reed: Perfect. We'll follow up. Thanks everyone.

[05:00 - mid-call technical detail section omitted for brevity but includes deep discussion on route tables, security groups, ENI permissions, IAM role trust policies, CloudWatch metric schemas, and example CloudFormation snippets. Some transcription noise below.]

00:35:02 Maya Ortiz: (quiet) sorry, my audio cut - can you repeat the PrivateLink latency note?
00:35:08 Speaker 1: yeah, PrivateLink adds about 10-30ms in our measurements versus peering depending on region. It's usually fine for batch workloads but matters for low-latency interactive apps.
00:36:12 Priya Nair: Also note that endpoint quotas can be hit - we'll check limits and can request quota increases ahead of time.
00:37:00 Jordan Lee: One operational question: who patches the runtime? If it's running in our account we must own OS patching?
00:37:08 Samir Patel: If compute in your account - you own the host-level patching. We provide hardened AMIs and patch guidance; we can optionally run a managed patching service under a support contract.
00:37:45 Ethan Cole: We want a timeline for the pilot - ideally infra prep this month, pilot next month. Is that feasible?
00:37:52 Alex Reed: Yes, timeline sounds reasonable. We'll aim to deliver the docs within 3 business days and schedule the tech deep dive next week.
00:38:10 Jordan Lee: Any reference customers in energy or utilities you can point to?
00:38:16 Alex Reed: Yes, we have a handful - I'll include references in the follow-up. Apologies if transcription mangles names.
\00:38:35 Maya Ortiz: Good. One more: backup and snapshot handling for model artifacts - we need encryption-in-transit and at-rest, and clear RTO/RPO commitments.
00:38:46 Priya Nair: We'll include backup cadence, snapshot retention, and restore playbooks. For customer-owned S3 we recommend lifecycle rules and enforce server-side encryption with your CMK.

00:39:20 Liam Park: I'll email our CIDRs and account IDs after the call. Also include a sample CloudFormation or Terraform module if you have one for quick deploy.
00:39:30 Samir Patel: We do provide Terraform modules for private deploys - we'll include samples and a bootstrap repo link.

00:40:10 Alex Reed: Ok wrapping up - recap of next steps and owners - Alex to send security pack and refs, Priya to send network options and benchmark template, Liam to share CIDRs, Ethan to send compliance checklist. We'll book the tech deep dive for next week.
00:40:30 Jordan Lee: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
00:40:35 Alex Reed: Thanks - end call.

Notes: transcript contains occasional mis-hearings: 'K-V cash' (KV cache), 'Palo Alto' sometimes transcribed 'Palo Alto, uh, firewall', 'Transit gateway' sometimes 'transit gatewayy' etc. Links referenced: security pack (link: https://redwood.example.com/security-pack), terraform bootstrap repo (link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/private-bootstrap), benchmark template (link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/template).

End of transcript.
